Her element, carried in her design: yttrium: a soft silvery metal, the first rare earth ever separated, drawn in 1794 from a heavy black stone found in a Swedish quarry that gave its name to four elements, yttrium the eldest; decades later its oxide was split again and two younger sisters were found hiding inside it; with aluminium it forms yttrium aluminium garnet, the clear crystal at the heart of powerful lasers that cut steel and of the fine green beams of eye surgery; with cerium it is the yellow phosphor that turns a blue LED warm white, with europium the red glow of screens; in 1987 it joined barium and copper in a ceramic that loses all electrical resistance at the temperature of liquid nitrogen, and it keeps zirconia from cracking.

3. COSTUME — FANTASY

Exposure (bold): her regalia opens to show skin — bare shoulders and arms between pauldron and bracer, a deep open neckline under the gorget with natural cleavage, a high slit in the tabard or robe showing the thigh; armor pieces stay on and symmetrical. Pose: standing confidently, her body turned slightly while her face looks toward the viewer.
Light: natural daylight or the world's own magical glow.
Composition: vertical 2:3 full-body framing with modest headroom and clear space below the boots — the whole figure from the top of her head or headpiece to both feet stays inside the frame, occupying about four-fifths of the image height, with the same camera distance in every world; her hands stay inside the frame. Camera level with her face with natural portrait perspective; her head level, chin neither raised nor tucked — no upward perspective on her face, no wide-angle distortion, no low angle, no close crop.

One figure only; no text or numbers except her element's own chemical symbol (Y) and atomic number (39) — and those only as part of the scene: engraved, embroidered or glowing on her costume, a banner, a sign or a machine, never as a floating label, corner badge, periodic-table tile, caption or overlay on the picture; no logo or watermark.
